## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated

  further pagination.
- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a

Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated
  (limit 1-100, default 20). Returns `ProjectRef` entries plus a `next_cursor` for
  further pagination.
- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a
  HyperFrames player widget that renders the project inline. Both the thumbnail
  and the preview HTML are regenerated server-side at request time.
- **get_project_status** — Text-only status check for an in-flight or finished
  project. Returns session_status (`p… [truncated]

 "sourceFile": "Use of extracorporeal shockwave therapies for athletes and physically active individuals - A systematic review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",

 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Use of extracorporeal shockwave therapies for athletes and physically active individuals: a systematic review' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Athletic Training"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Injured Athletes", "Adult / Recreational", "Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "PRISMA systematic review of four databases (searched April 2023) covering 56 studies with 1874 athletes or physically active individuals, including 18 level I studies. Findings were synthesised narratively because heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis; the authors report ESWT may be effective alone for plantar fasciitis, lateral epicondylitis and proximal hamstring tendinopathy, and as an adjunct to exercise for medial tibial stress syndrome and osteitis pubis, with mostly low-level evidence for patellar tendinopathy.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Narrative synthesis only, with heterogeneous comparators, doses and outcomes; 25 of 56 included studies were case series or reports with positive outcomes. Only 20 of 56 studies reported adverse events and the review was restricted to English-language publications.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the review as proof that ESWT speeds return to sport across injuries, when the level I evidence covers only a few conditions and the authors say the benefit over exercise alone is uncertain for patellar tendinopathy.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Rhim HC, Shin J, Kang J, et al. Use of extracorporeal shockwave therapies for athletes and physically active individuals: a systematic review. Br J Sports Med. 2024;0:1-12.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2023-107567",
  "abstract": "The review examined the efficacy of extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) and outcomes for athletes and physically active individuals across 56 included studies. The authors found the strongest support for plantar fasciitis, lateral epicondylitis and proximal hamstring tendinopathy, and for adjunct use in medial tibial stress syndrome and osteitis pubis.",
  "tldr": "ESWT looks effective alone for a few sports injuries and as an add-on to exercise for others, but most of the evidence is low level. Use it as one option to discuss with athletes, not as a general return-to-sport treatment.",
  "methods": "The authors followed PRISMA and searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL and Web of Science in April 2023. They included RCTs, cohort, case-control, case series and case reports of ESWT in athletes, physically active adults and military cadets, and synthesised results narratively because the studies were too heterogeneous to pool.",
  "findings": "Of 56 studies with 1874 participants, 18 were level I. Patellar tendinopathy was the most studied condition, with conflicting RCT results. Level I RCTs supported ESWT alone for plantar fasciitis, lateral epicondylitis and proximal hamstring tendinopathy, and ESWT added to exercise for medial tibial stress syndrome and osteitis pubis. Adverse events were mostly temporary pain and erythema, and were reported in 20 of 56 studies.",
  "limitations": "No meta-analysis was possible, and 25 of the 56 studies were case series or reports, which the authors say should be interpreted with caution. Adverse-event reporting was incomplete, and only English-language studies were included.",
  "practicalImplications": "Consider ESWT for plantar fasciitis, lateral epicondylitis and proximal hamstring tendinopathy, or as an add-on to exercise for medial tibial stress syndrome and osteitis pubis. Do not expect it to add benefit to eccentric loading for patellar tendinopathy.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: ESWT can often be given with training and competition continuing as tolerated, which may suit in-season athletes. Keep it inside a structured load plan, because the review found no clear advantage over exercise alone for patellar tendinopathy.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review reports return to sport within weeks in several level I and case-series studies, such as about 6 weeks in some hamstring and tibial stress cases. Treat these as variable, low-level estimates. The review does not provide validated return-to-sport criteria after ESWT."
 }
}

12	Ludovica Verde4 , Annamaria Colao5,6,7 , Henry Lukaski8 , Daniel Simancas-Racines9† ,

16	    Abstract
17	    The use of bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) is now well established in healthcare as an essential support
18	    tool for patient management in various clinical settings. Its use in sports is rapidly expanding due to the
19	    valuable insights it offers, helping to better structure athletes’ diets and training programs, thereby optimizing
20	    their performance. In the context of sport, however, there is a consensus regarding the importance of proper
21	    interpretation of BIA-derived data, which cannot be limited to mere estimation of body composition. In this sense,
22	    therefore, the evaluation and interpretation of raw bioelectrical parameters, including resistance, reactance, and
23	    phase angle (PhA) is of relevant importance. The assessment of PhA is particularly significant in the context of
24	    sports, as it is closely linked to key factors such as muscle mass, strength, and overall muscle quality. However,
25	    the existing relationship between PhA and systemic, and loco-regional inflammation, which, in a broader sense,
26	    is the rationale behind its use for assessing and monitoring localised muscle damage. Thus, the importance of
27	    PhA monitoring during training becomes evident, as it plays a crucial role in assessing and potentially identifying
28	    functional impairments, such as overtraining syndrome, as well as muscle injury and related changes in fluid
29	    distribution, at an early stage. The aim of this review is to provide the scientific basis necessary to consider the use
30	    of whole-body PhA as an indicator of overtraining.
31	    Keywords BIA, BIVA, Overreaching, Fatigue, Inflammation, Overtraining, Acute and chronic fatigue

Use of phase angle as an indicator
of overtraining in sport and physical training
Giuseppe Annunziata1† , Antonio Paoli2† , Evelyn Frias-Toral3† , Stellario Marra1, Francesco Campa2 ,
Ludovica Verde4 , Annamaria Colao5,6,7 , Henry Lukaski8 , Daniel Simancas-Racines9† ,
Giovanna Muscogiuri5,6,7† and Luigi Barrea10*†


    Abstract
    The use of bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) is now well established in healthcare as an essential support
    tool for patient management in various clinical settings. Its use in sports is rapidly expanding due to the
    valuable insights it offers, helping to better structure athletes’ diets and training programs, thereby optimizing
    their performance. In the context of sport, however, there is a consensus regarding the importance of proper
    interpretation of BIA-derived data, which cannot be limited to mere estimation of body composition. In this sense,
    therefore, the evaluation and interpretation of raw bioelectrical parameters, including resistance, reactance, and
    phase angle (PhA) is of relevant importance. The assessment of PhA is particularly significant in the context of
    sports, as it is closely linked to key factors such as muscle mass, strength, and overall muscle quality. However,
    the existing relationship between PhA and systemic, and loco-regional inflammation, which, in a broader sense,
    is the rationale behind its use for assessing and monitoring localised muscle damage. Thus, the importance of
    PhA monitoring during training becomes evident, as it plays a crucial role in assessing and potentially identifying
    functional impairments, such as overtraining syndrome, as well as muscle injury and related changes in fluid
    distribution, at an early stage. The aim of this review is to provide the scientific basis necessary to consider the use
    of whole-body PhA as an indicator of overtraining.
    Keywords BIA, BIVA, Overreaching, Fatigue, Inflammation, Overtraining, Acute and chronic fatigue

{
 "id": "Q28",
 "sourceFile": "Use of phase angle as an indicator of overtraining in sport and physical training.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Use of phase angle as an indicator of overtraining in sport and physical training' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Recovery & Readiness", "Training & Performance"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Nutrition", "Coaching"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport", "Endurance Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) raw parameters, focusing on phase angle (PhA), and how PhA relates to muscle mass, resistance training, inflammation, oxidative stress and overreaching or overtraining. No search method is described, and the authors state that no study has measured PhA directly under overtraining syndrome conditions. They propose PhA as a possible prognostic marker of overtraining risk, based on theory and indirect evidence.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review is a theoretical narrative without a described search, and the central hypothesis is untested in athletes. The evidence is mostly from clinical, elderly or healthy non-athlete samples, and the paper itself calls its conclusions speculative.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could take the proposed PhA-overtraining link as a validated monitoring tool and set PhA cut-offs or act on single PhA changes, when the authors describe it only as a hypothesis for future testing.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Annunziata G, Paoli A, Frias-Toral E, et al. Use of phase angle as an indicator of overtraining in sport and physical training. J Transl Med. 2024;22:1084.",
  "doi": "10.1186/s12967-024-05918-w",
  "abstract": "The authors review the use of raw bioelectrical impedance parameters, especially phase angle, in sport and propose PhA as an indicator of overtraining. They link PhA to muscle mass, fitness, inflammation and oxidative stress, and argue it could detect overreaching early.",
  "tldr": "Phase angle from BIA may reflect cell health, muscle quality and inflammation, so it could be a useful trend to watch alongside training load. Its use for detecting overtraining is still a hypothesis without athlete-specific validation.",
  "methods": "This is a narrative review. The article does not describe a systematic search or selection process, and it draws on prior reviews, meta-analyses and mechanistic studies on BIA, PhA, resistance training and inflammation.",
  "findings": "The review reports that PhA is higher in trained athletes than in non-athletes and tends to rise with resistance training in the studies cited, mostly through changes in resistance and muscle hydration. PhA has been linked to inflammatory markers and to fitness in non-athlete samples. The authors state that no study has measured PhA directly under overtraining syndrome, and they propose that a sudden fall in PhA during training could signal overtraining.",
  "limitations": "The review is not systematic, and most cited evidence comes from clinical, elderly or non-athlete populations. The authors state that the athlete-specific evidence, the overreaching and overtraining definitions, and the validated protocols are all lacking. The proposed prognostic use is explicitly speculative.",
  "practicalImplications": "Measure PhA with consistent BIA protocols and track it over time alongside training load, performance and mood. Interpret a sudden fall in PhA as a prompt to review load and recovery, not as a diagnosis of overtraining.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Monitoring PhA trends over a season may help coaches and nutrition staff see when body-cell mass or fluid balance is shifting alongside load. The review does not give validated PhA thresholds or training-load rules, so it cannot set training prescriptions.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review does not study return to sport or injury recovery in a way that can inform return-to-play decisions. It can at most suggest that PhA could reflect muscle damage or fluid change after injury, which would need separate study."
 }
}

The authors state that the athlete-specific evidence, the overreaching and overtraining definitions, and the validated protocols are all lacking. The proposed prognostic use is explicitly speculative.",
  "practicalImplications": "Measure PhA with consistent BIA protocols and track it over time alongside training load, performance and mood. Interpret a sudden fall in PhA as a prompt to review load and recovery, not as a diagnosis of overtraining.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Monitoring PhA trends over a season may help coaches and nutrition staff see when body-cell mass or fluid balance is shifting alongside load. The review does not give validated PhA thresholds or training-load rules, so it cannot set training prescriptions.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review does not study return to sport or injury recovery in a way that can inform return-to-play decisions. It can at most suggest that PhA could reflect muscle damage or fluid change after injury, which would need separate study."

 "evidenceSummary": "PRISMA-guided systematic review and bibliometric analysis of 209 studies published 2000 to 2022 that relied solely on publicly obtained data (online reports, media and team sites) on collegiate, semiprofessional and professional athletes. and Robert W. Keneficka

    ABSTRACT                                                                                                      ARTICLE HISTORY
    Exercise or work in hot environments increases susceptibility to exertional heat illnesses such as            Received 5 September 2018
    exertional heat stroke (EHS). EHS occurs when body heat gain exceeds body heat dissipation,                   Revised 12 December 2018
    resulting in rapid body heat storage and potentially life-threatening consequences. EHS poses                 Accepted 15 December 2018
    a dangerous threat for athletes, agriculture workers, and military personnel, as they are often               KEYWORDS
    exposed to hot environmental conditions that restrict body heat loss or contribute to body heat               Exertional heat stroke; heat
    gain. Currently, there is limited guidance on return to activity (RTA) after an episode of EHS. While         tolerance test; heat illness;
    examining biomarkers in the blood is thought to be beneficial for determining RTA, they are not               return to play; return to duty
    sensitive or specific enough to be a final determining factor as organ damage may persist despite
    blood biomarkers returning to baseline levels. As such, additional assessment tests to more
    accurately determine RTA are desired. One method used for determining RTA is the heat tolerance
    test (HTT, 120 minutes treadmill walking; 40°C, 40% relative humidity). Unfortunately, the HTT
    provides even less information about EHS recovery since it offers no test sensitivity or specificity
    even after years of implementation. We provide an overview of the HTT and the controversy of
    this test with respect to assessment criteria, applicability to tasks involving high metabolic work-
    loads, and the lack of follow-up analyses to determine its accuracy for determining recovery in
    order to diminish the likelihood of a second EHS occurrence.

97	                                                       Large-scale epidemiological studies have estimated the expected RTS time for major
98	                                                   injuries in football at the population level accounting for associated injury risk factors[6–10].
99	                                                   These studies describe the risk factors for a disease or injury and the extent of the problem.
100	                                                   Medical staff can then use an “anchor and adjust” strategy to optimise predictive accuracy,
101	                                                   thus better estimating RTS times[11]. While typical epidemiological studies aim to estimate
102	                                                   population-level effect and trends, tools to translate population-level data into individual-level
103	                                                   estimations would be helpful.
104	                                                       Forecasting the time to RTS based on individual characteristics can be challenging for several
105	                                                   reasons. First, the Strategic Assessment of Risk and Risk Tolerance Framework recommends
106	                                                   considering personal characteristics and factors, such as age and playing position[12]. However,
107	                                                   quantifying and synthesising this information in the clinical reasoning process can be difficult.
108	                                                   For example, what is the difference between the rehabilitation time required for a 20-year-old
109	                                                   striker versus a 30-year-old defender with a same type of hamstring strain injury? Second,
110	                                                   synthesising useful information from broad population-level epidemiological data covering
111	                                                   entire leagues and multiple seasons and then personalising it to a specific player-context is
112	                                                   almost cognitively infeasible for a single individual or even a small group of individuals. There
113	                                                   are no tools to help translate the sheer volume and complexity of the population-level data and
114	                                                   tailor them to an individual level. Third, medical staff, like any other humans, are susceptible to
115	                                                   various decision-making challenges. They have limited information processing capacity[13] and
116	                                                   face potential cognitive biases[14,15]. Human judgment can be vulnerable, particularly when it
117	                                                   comes to statistical and probabilistic reasoning[16]. Without an objective and reliable decision-­
118	                                                   making tool specifically designed to provide individualised RTS estimations, medical staff often
119	                                                   rely heavily on their clinical experience and population-level epidemiological data.
120	                                                       Data scientists have the potential to develop decision support tools that can effectively
121	                                                   synthesise broad epidemiological data and personalise it to specific player-contexts, overcom-
122	                                                   ing the cognitive limitations faced by individuals. These tools can provide valuable additional
123	                                                   information that would otherwise be challenging for a single human to process. In practical
124	                                                   settings, data scientists can undertake the setting up and maintaining the decision support
125	                                                   tool, while users such as medical staff and coaches utilise the tool in planning for an athlete’s

137	                                               Developing a computer-based decision support tool that uses a complex systems approach
138	                                           may be helpful to overcome the previous challenges and offer a competitive advantage in
139	                                           forecasting RTS[17]. Specifically, the key differentiator of a complex systems approach in RTS
140	                                           is the explicit modelling of factor interactions that could be queried and used by medical staff
141	                                           in multiple ways. This includes, but is not limited to understanding the strength of influence
142	                                           of different variables and predicting the outcome based on custom RTS scenarios.
143	                                               Computer-based decision support tools can be divided into predictive and descriptive
144	                                           modelling[18]. Predictive modelling can be used for injury diagnosis, severity estimation, and
145	                                           rehabilitation planning. In particular, the Bayesian network (BN) is well suited for providing
146	                                           injury prognosis in sports, due to its capacity to model complex systems and to integrate clin-
147	                                           ical data, non-clinical factors and expert knowledge. However, it has not been previously used
148	                                           for such a purpose.
149	
150	                                           About the Bayesian network
151	                                           A BN is a graph-based modelling method where the relationships between variables (nodes)
152	                                           are represented with arrows (arcs) (See Fig 1). The presence of an arc denotes the influence of
153	                                           one node on another, and the absence of one assumes conditional independence[19]. While
154	                                           real data often contains a mixture of discrete and continuous variables, BN structure learn-
155	                                           ing algorithms often assume the random variables are discrete. This type of BN is called the
156	                                           discrete BN, which involves discretising continuous variables in the dataset into categories.
157	                                           Although some information is lost when continuous data are categorised[20], there are merits
158	                                           of using the discrete Bayesian network that are worth discussing.
159	                                               In practical settings, people often find it easier to work with discrete representations rather
160	                                           than continuous data. Discrete variables tend to be more interpretable, facilitating abstract
161	                                           reasoning[21]. For example, word tokens often enable fast and exact processing[21]. Consider
162	                                           the comparison between the words “tall” and “short” versus the numerical values “183cm”
163	                                           and “150cm”. Some may find the descriptive terms are easier to grasp and apply in reasoning.
164	                                           Given the complexity of the human body and interacting processes involved in RTS, discre-
165	                                           tisation may help capture the resolution of the data available and its relevance to the decision
166	                                           support scenario at hand[22].
167	                                               However, it’s also important to note the disadvantages to discretising continuous vari-
168	                                           ables[23]. Discretisation can lead to information loss, as the finer details and nuances captured
169	                                           by continuous data may be overlooked. By converting continuous variables into discrete
170	                                           categories, we sacrifice the precision and granularity inherent in the original data. Addition-
171	                                           ally, the choice of how to discretise the variables can introduce subjectivity and bias into the
172	                                           analysis and therefore, it is crucial to ensure transparency in how variables are discretised to
173	                                           mitigate these potential issues.
174	                                               BNs provide a platform for inferring state probabilities given observations, referred to as
175	                                           evidence, of one or more nodes in the network. In the discrete BN, the relationship between
176	                                           parent nodes and a child node can be quantified using conditional probability tables (CPTs).
177	                                           The CPT reflects the probability of child node states (or outcomes) given every possible com-
178	                                           bination of parent node states[24]. As new evidence comes in, changes may be made to the
179	                                           node’s marginal probability[25], which is known as the posterior probability. The posterior
180	                                           probability is the updated probability of a hypothesis or event after considering new evidence.
181	                                           They combine prior beliefs with the likelihood of the data to provide an updated estimate of
182	                                           the event’s probability.

191	                                              BNs can perform both predictive and diagnostic inference. For example, medical staff
192	                                           can use the former to predict the outcome of an injury for a given clinical diagnosis,
193	                                           anthropometric and match factors (predictive inference); but can also enter the injury
194	                                           severity as an observation to examine what injury factors could explain that observation
195	                                           (diagnostic inference). As an important feature to end users who may not be familiar with
196	                                           statistics, the BN provides visuals to facilitate understanding and supporting decision mak-
197	                                           ing across teams of users, such as, among athletes, coaching staff, medical and non-medical
198	                                           personnel.
199	                                              Another key feature of a BN is that medical staff can integrate and visualise data from
200	                                           multiple sources into a single BN, such as clinical data, empirical evidence and expert knowl-
201	                                           edge[26], or combinations of these[27]. Expert knowledge can be invaluable when empirical
202	                                           data is scarce or unavailable. It also plays a significant role in developing models, selecting
203	                                           data or variables, estimating parameters, interpreting results and determining the uncertainty
204	                                           characteristics. Since the BN can be customised based on the experts’ knowledge[28,29], it
205	                                           may be appealing for small sample size research in elite sports research[30–32], where some
206	                                           data may be missing or not be feasible to collect (e.g., limitations in applied settings)[26].
207	                                           BNs have been used to support clinical decisions[33–36], analyse complex systems in ecology
208	                                           [22,37,38] and logistics[39].
209	
210	                                           Study objectives
211	                                           The objective of this study was to demonstrate the use of a Bayesian network and its potential
212	                                           utility in becoming a decision support tool for medical staff for RTS. Specifically, a discrete
213	                                           BN was modelled based on a set of basic epidemiological data to demonstrate how medical
214	                                           staff can use BN to understand 1) the most influential variable to the outcomes, 2) the strength
215	                                           of influence of different variables, and to 3) demonstrate its use with a case scenario.

220	                                           professional men’s highest football league (Bundesliga) between 2014/2015–2020/2021.
221	                                           Neither research ethics board approval nor a trial registration was required as all data were
222	                                           collected from publicly available sources[9,40]. We reported the result with reference to the
223	                                           Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diag-
224	                                           nosis (TRIPOD) statement[41].

243	                                                    Participants
244	                                                    Players who played in the Bundesliga in the above-mentioned seven seasons were included in
245	                                                    the study. Injured players who did not return to the Bundesliga in the same season and those
246	                                                    without complete data were excluded from the analysis. All participants were identified using
247	                                                    a publicly available database, including Kicker SportmagazinTM, and clubs’ official websites.
248	                                                    Data collection was performed via methods established in previous investigations[9,42]. The
249	                                                    data has been collected according to the Fuller et al. consensus statement for football injury
250	                                                    research and the same definitions have been the same throughout the 7 seasons[43]. 3374
251	                                                    player Bundesliga seasons were registered over the seven seasons from 2014/2015–2020/2021.
252	                                                    A total of 6653 time-loss injuries were recorded. After removing injuries without complete
253	                                                    data, 6143 time-loss injuries remained.

255	                                                    Construction of the Bayesian network
256	                                                    The modelling process and validation were performed in GeNIe 2.0 (Bayes Fusion, LLC)[44].
257	                                                    There are four main steps to creating and validating a BN:
258	                                                    1) Identify the variables (nodes) of the BN and the key response variables. In this study,
259	                                                       the key response variables are the (i) severity of the injury (severity) and (ii) days to RTS
260	                                                       (days_rts). They are used to evaluate the performance of the BN. The nodes and sources of
261	                                                       information are outlined in Table 1.
262	                                                    2) Learn the graphical structure of the BN and display the relationships between all the nodes.
263	                                                    3) Learn the probability distribution governing the relationships between the nodes.
264	                                                    4) Validate the BN to evaluate how well the BN can classify injury based on the key response
265	                                                       variables: (i) severity and (ii) days_rts.
266	                                                       Step 1: Identify the main variables. This model is intended to capture the conditional
267	                                                    probabilistic relationships among personal characteristics, match and injury information.
268	                                                    The variables in this study are commonly included in epidemiologic studies[45] and we have
269	                                                    summarised them in Table 1.
270	                                                       All time-loss injuries that occurred during football competitions and training sessions were
271	                                                    included, and the day of the injury is counted as day zero. A time-loss injury is when a player
272	                                                    cannot fully participate in training or competition due to injury[43]. RTS is defined as when
273	                                                    the player has received medical clearance to allow full participation in training and is available

315	                                           the search to help ensure graph structures produced are consistent with clinical science
316	                                           (See S1 Fig). We first specified the temporal order of the variables, ensuring there were no
317	                                           arcs from variables that occurred later (e.g., injury) to nodes happening earlier (e.g., main
318	                                           playing position). Following this, Author KY established the relationships (arcs) within the
319	                                           graphical structure. Notably, the key response variable, days_rts, was directly linked to severity
320	                                           in the graphical structure. This mapping was based on the definition of severity outlined in
321	                                           the Fuller et al. consensus statement on football injury studies, which defines severity by the
322	                                           duration of unavailability for full training[43]. This mapping was done manually based on
323	                                           clinical knowledge and could not be learnt from algorithms. Finally, with the constraints in
324	                                           place, we used the Bayesian Search algorithm in GeNIe 2.0 to find the best-fitted network
325	                                           for the optimal network configuration that aligns with the collected data and expert
326	                                           knowledge[19,47].
327	                                               Step 3: Define the probability distribution. There are multiple ways to discretise
328	                                           continuous data, including manual, unsupervised and supervised. Each method offers distinct
329	                                           advantages, such as improved model performance, easier interpretation, and computational
330	                                           efficiency[48]. Manual discretisation involves manually defining thresholds or categories to
331	                                           discretise the continuous data. This approach provides flexibility and allows domain experts to
332	                                           incorporate their knowledge, ensuring that the categories align with relevant domain-specific
333	                                           consensus statements and the specific needs of the analysis. Unsupervised discretisation
334	                                           involves using clustering algorithms to identify natural groupings or patterns in the data.
335	                                           These clusters can then be treated as discrete categories. This is particularly useful when prior
336	                                           knowledge or predefined categories are unavailable[49]. Supervised discretisation utilises
337	                                           labelled data to guide the discretisation process. Machine learning algorithms or decision
338	                                           trees can be employed to learn optimal thresholds or categories that maximise predictive
339	                                           performance. This method can enhance both model performance and interpretability[49].
340	                                               We manually discretised the continuous data based on domain-specific decision categories
341	                                           to maximise usability across various practitioner types and clubs. Specifically, the continuous
342	                                           data are discretised based on categories that are easy to apply practically or with reference to
343	                                           relevant consensus statements. We discretised age, height, and weight into three categories that
344	                                           represents the typical values observed in the sample, to create uniform count categories that
345	                                           were both meaningful and easy to interpret. severity was discretised based on the Fuller et al.
346	                                           consensus of epidemiological data collection into four categories (minimal, mild, moderate
347	                                           and severe)[43]. days_rts was discretised into six categories: 1–3, 4–7, 8–14, 15–28, 29–60,
348	                                           > 60 days, with reference to the Fuller et al. consensus of epidemiological data collection[43].

                                                       Large-scale epidemiological studies have estimated the expected RTS time for major
                                                   injuries in football at the population level accounting for associated injury risk factors[6–10].
                                                   These studies describe the risk factors for a disease or injury and the extent of the problem.
                                                   Medical staff can then use an “anchor and adjust” strategy to optimise predictive accuracy,
                                                   thus better estimating RTS times[11]. While typical epidemiological studies aim to estimate
                                                   population-level effect and trends, tools to translate population-level data into individual-level

                                                       Forecasting the time to RTS based on individual characteristics can be challenging for several
                                                   reasons. First, the Strategic Assessment of Risk and Risk Tolerance Framework recommends
                                                   considering personal characteristics and factors, such as age and playing position[12]. However,

                                                   For example, what is the difference between the rehabilitation time required for a 20-year-old
                                                   striker versus a 30-year-old defender with a same type of hamstring strain injury? Second,
                                                   synthesising useful information from broad population-level epidemiological data covering
                                                   entire leagues and multiple seasons and then personalising it to a specific player-context is
                                                   almost cognitively infeasible for a single individual or even a small group of individuals. There
                                                   are no tools to help translate the sheer volume and complexity of the population-level data and
                                                   tailor them to an individual level. Third, medical staff, like any other humans, are susceptible to
                                                   various decision-making challenges. They have limited information processing capacity[13] and
                                                   face potential cognitive biases[14,15]. Human judgment can be vulnerable, particularly when it
                                                   comes to statistical and probabilistic reasoning[16]. Without an objective and reliable decision-­
                                                   making tool specifically designed to provide individualised RTS estimations, medical staff often
                                                   rely heavily on their clinical experience and population-level epidemiological data.
                                                       Data scientists have the potential to develop decision support tools that can effectively
                                                   synthesise broad epidemiological data and personalise it to specific player-contexts, overcom-
                                                   ing the cognitive limitations faced by individuals. These tools can provide valuable additional
                                                   information that would otherwise be challenging for a single human to process. In practical
                                                   settings, data scientists can undertake the setting up and maintaining the decision support
                                                   tool, while users such as medical staff and coaches utilise the tool in planning for an athlete’s

                                           RTS, making necessary adjustments for the team, and ensuring the team remains competitive.
                                           This collaboration between data scientists and end users can lead to more informed decision-­
                                           making and strategic planning.
                                               Developing a computer-based decision support tool that uses a complex systems approach
                                           may be helpful to overcome the previous challenges and offer a competitive advantage in
                                           forecasting RTS[17]. Specifically, the key differentiator of a complex systems approach in RTS
                                           is the explicit modelling of factor interactions that could be queried and used by medical staff
                                           in multiple ways. This includes, but is not limited to understanding the strength of influence
                                           of different variables and predicting the outcome based on custom RTS scenarios.
                                               Computer-based decision support tools can be divided into predictive and descriptive
                                           modelling[18]. Predictive modelling can be used for injury diagnosis, severity estimation, and
                                           rehabilitation planning. In particular, the Bayesian network (BN) is well suited for providing
                                           injury prognosis in sports, due to its capacity to model complex systems and to integrate clin-
                                           ical data, non-clinical factors and expert knowledge. However, it has not been previously used
                                           for such a purpose.

                                           About the Bayesian network
                                           A BN is a graph-based modelling method where the relationships between variables (nodes)
                                           are represented with arrows (arcs) (See Fig 1). The presence of an arc denotes the influence of
                                           one node on another, and the absence of one assumes conditional independence[19]. While
                                           real data often contains a mixture of discrete and continuous variables, BN structure learn-
                                           ing algorithms often assume the random variables are discrete. This type of BN is called the
                                           discrete BN, which involves discretising continuous variables in the dataset into categories.
                                           Although some information is lost when continuous data are categorised[20], there are merits
                                           of using the discrete Bayesian network that are worth discussing.
                                               In practical settings, people often find it easier to work with discrete representations rather
                                           than continuous data. Discrete variables tend to be more interpretable, facilitating abstract
                                           reasoning[21]. For example, word tokens often enable fast and exact processing[21]. Consider
                                           the comparison between the words “tall” and “short” versus the numerical values “183cm”
                                           and “150cm”. Some may find the descriptive terms are easier to grasp and apply in reasoning.
                                           Given the complexity of the human body and interacting processes involved in RTS, discre-
                                           tisation may help capture the resolution of the data available and its relevance to the decision
                                           support scenario at hand[22].
                                               However, it’s also important to note the disadvantages to discretising continuous vari-
                                           ables[23]. Discretisation can lead to information loss, as the finer details and nuances captured
                                           by continuous data may be overlooked. By converting continuous variables into discrete
                                           categories, we sacrifice the precision and granularity inherent in the original data. Addition-
                                           ally, the choice of how to discretise the variables can introduce subjectivity and bias into the
                                           analysis and therefore, it is crucial to ensure transparency in how variables are discretised to
                                           mitigate these potential issues.
                                               BNs provide a platform for inferring state probabilities given observations, referred to as
                                           evidence, of one or more nodes in the network. In the discrete BN, the relationship between
                                           parent nodes and a child node can be quantified using conditional probability tables (CPTs).
                                           The CPT reflects the probability of child node states (or outcomes) given every possible com-
                                           bination of parent node states[24]. As new evidence comes in, changes may be made to the
                                           node’s marginal probability[25], which is known as the posterior probability. The posterior
                                           probability is the updated probability of a hypothesis or event after considering new evidence.
                                           They combine prior beliefs with the likelihood of the data to provide an updated estimate of
                                           the event’s probability.

 PLOS ONE                                                                                         Using a Bayesian network to classify time to return to sport



                                              BNs can perform both predictive and diagnostic inference. For example, medical staff
                                           can use the former to predict the outcome of an injury for a given clinical diagnosis,
                                           anthropometric and match factors (predictive inference); but can also enter the injury
                                           severity as an observation to examine what injury factors could explain that observation
                                           (diagnostic inference). As an important feature to end users who may not be familiar with
                                           statistics, the BN provides visuals to facilitate understanding and supporting decision mak-
                                           ing across teams of users, such as, among athletes, coaching staff, medical and non-medical
                                           personnel.
                                              Another key feature of a BN is that medical staff can integrate and visualise data from
                                           multiple sources into a single BN, such as clinical data, empirical evidence and expert knowl-
                                           edge[26], or combinations of these[27]. Expert knowledge can be invaluable when empirical
                                           data is scarce or unavailable. It also plays a significant role in developing models, selecting
                                           data or variables, estimating parameters, interpreting results and determining the uncertainty
                                           characteristics. Since the BN can be customised based on the experts’ knowledge[28,29], it
                                           may be appealing for small sample size research in elite sports research[30–32], where some
                                           data may be missing or not be feasible to collect (e.g., limitations in applied settings)[26].
                                           BNs have been used to support clinical decisions[33–36], analyse complex systems in ecology
                                           [22,37,38] and logistics[39].

                                           Study objectives
                                           The objective of this study was to demonstrate the use of a Bayesian network and its potential
                                           utility in becoming a decision support tool for medical staff for RTS. Specifically, a discrete
                                           BN was modelled based on a set of basic epidemiological data to demonstrate how medical
                                           staff can use BN to understand 1) the most influential variable to the outcomes, 2) the strength
                                           of influence of different variables, and to 3) demonstrate its use with a case scenario.

                                           Materials and methods
                                           Study design
                                           The study is a retrospective analysis of prospectively collected injury data from the German
                                           professional men’s highest football league (Bundesliga) between 2014/2015–2020/2021.
                                           Neither research ethics board approval nor a trial registration was required as all data were
                                           collected from publicly available sources[9,40]. We reported the result with reference to the
                                           Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diag-
                                           nosis (TRIPOD) statement[41].

                                           while B, C, D, E and F are the descendants of A; and so on. The arrows indicate the direction of influence.

                                                    Participants
                                                    Players who played in the Bundesliga in the above-mentioned seven seasons were included in
                                                    the study. Injured players who did not return to the Bundesliga in the same season and those
                                                    without complete data were excluded from the analysis. All participants were identified using
                                                    a publicly available database, including Kicker SportmagazinTM, and clubs’ official websites.
                                                    Data collection was performed via methods established in previous investigations[9,42]. The
                                                    data has been collected according to the Fuller et al. consensus statement for football injury
                                                    research and the same definitions have been the same throughout the 7 seasons[43]. 3374
                                                    player Bundesliga seasons were registered over the seven seasons from 2014/2015–2020/2021.
                                                    A total of 6653 time-loss injuries were recorded. After removing injuries without complete
                                                    data, 6143 time-loss injuries remained.

                                                    Construction of the Bayesian network
                                                    The modelling process and validation were performed in GeNIe 2.0 (Bayes Fusion, LLC)[44].
                                                    There are four main steps to creating and validating a BN:
                                                    1) Identify the variables (nodes) of the BN and the key response variables. In this study,
                                                       the key response variables are the (i) severity of the injury (severity) and (ii) days to RTS
                                                       (days_rts). They are used to evaluate the performance of the BN. The nodes and sources of
                                                       information are outlined in Table 1.
                                                    2) Learn the graphical structure of the BN and display the relationships between all the nodes.
                                                    3) Learn the probability distribution governing the relationships between the nodes.
                                                    4) Validate the BN to evaluate how well the BN can classify injury based on the key response
                                                       variables: (i) severity and (ii) days_rts.
                                                       Step 1: Identify the main variables. This model is intended to capture the conditional
                                                    probabilistic relationships among personal characteristics, match and injury information.
                                                    The variables in this study are commonly included in epidemiologic studies[45] and we have
                                                    summarised them in Table 1.
                                                       All time-loss injuries that occurred during football competitions and training sessions were
                                                    included, and the day of the injury is counted as day zero. A time-loss injury is when a player
                                                    cannot fully participate in training or competition due to injury[43]. RTS is defined as when
                                                    the player has received medical clearance to allow full participation in training and is available

                                               We are interested in determining the days to RTS, therefore, the two key response variables
                                           in this model are injury severity (severity) and days to RTS (days_rts). Injury severity (sever-
                                           ity) was categorised according to the days of absence in match or training as outlined by the
                                           Fuller et al. consensus statement on football injury studies[43]: minimal (1–3 days), mild (4–7
                                           days), moderate (8–28 days), or severe (>28 days). We further create a new variable based on
                                           days to RTS (days_rts) to evaluate if the model could classify the days to RTS into more pre-
                                           cise categories. There are two additional categories in days_rts as compared to severity: 1–3,
                                           4–7, 8–14, 15–28, 29–60, > 60 days. In context, these variables form the nodes in the BN. A
                                           summary of the variables and source of the data are presented in Table 1.
                                               Step 2: Define the graphical structure. We incorporated expert knowledge to constrain
                                           the search to help ensure graph structures produced are consistent with clinical science
                                           (See S1 Fig). We first specified the temporal order of the variables, ensuring there were no
                                           arcs from variables that occurred later (e.g., injury) to nodes happening earlier (e.g., main
                                           playing position). Following this, Author KY established the relationships (arcs) within the
                                           graphical structure. Notably, the key response variable, days_rts, was directly linked to severity
                                           in the graphical structure. This mapping was based on the definition of severity outlined in
                                           the Fuller et al. consensus statement on football injury studies, which defines severity by the
                                           duration of unavailability for full training[43]. This mapping was done manually based on
                                           clinical knowledge and could not be learnt from algorithms. Finally, with the constraints in
                                           place, we used the Bayesian Search algorithm in GeNIe 2.0 to find the best-fitted network
                                           for the optimal network configuration that aligns with the collected data and expert
                                           knowledge[19,47].
                                               Step 3: Define the probability distribution. There are multiple ways to discretise
                                           continuous data, including manual, unsupervised and supervised. Each method offers distinct
                                           advantages, such as improved model performance, easier interpretation, and computational
                                           efficiency[48]. Manual discretisation involves manually defining thresholds or categories to
                                           discretise the continuous data. This approach provides flexibility and allows domain experts to
                                           incorporate their knowledge, ensuring that the categories align with relevant domain-specific
                                           consensus statements and the specific needs of the analysis. Unsupervised discretisation
                                           involves using clustering algorithms to identify natural groupings or patterns in the data.
                                           These clusters can then be treated as discrete categories. This is particularly useful when prior
                                           knowledge or predefined categories are unavailable[49]. Supervised discretisation utilises
                                           labelled data to guide the discretisation process. Machine learning algorithms or decision
                                           trees can be employed to learn optimal thresholds or categories that maximise predictive
                                           performance. This method can enhance both model performance and interpretability[49].
                                               We manually discretised the continuous data based on domain-specific decision categories
                                           to maximise usability across various practitioner types and clubs. Specifically, the continuous
                                           data are discretised based on categories that are easy to apply practically or with reference to
                                           relevant consensus statements. We discretised age, height, and weight into three categories that
                                           represents the typical values observed in the sample, to create uniform count categories that
                                           were both meaningful and easy to interpret. severity was discretised based on the Fuller et al.
                                           consensus of epidemiological data collection into four categories (minimal, mild, moderate
                                           and severe)[43]. days_rts was discretised into six categories: 1–3, 4–7, 8–14, 15–28, 29–60,
                                           > 60 days, with reference to the Fuller et al. consensus of epidemiological data collection[43].
