521	                                                    In this model, we use a hybrid approach in constructing the BN; that is, we have combined
522	                                                    clinical knowledge and data-driven learning (Bayesian Search algorithm) when construct-
523	                                                    ing the graphical structure. This is because constructing the BN using pure algorithmic
524	                                                    approaches (i.e., unsupervised learning) can sometimes produce graph structures with unrea-
525	                                                    sonable arcs, such as the model attempting to explain age with severity. However, if we use a
526	                                                    pure domain approach, we may miss some of the patterns and linkages between variables that
527	                                                    were not observed by clinicians. Therefore, we opted to use a hybrid approach when con-
528	                                                    structing the BN.
529	                                                         The BN model may help medical staff working in the Bundesliga to view athletes and
530	                                                    ­injuries with a complex systems approach. For example, the model captured the complex
531	                                                     relationships between the time of the season, the injury type and injury occurrence (Fig 2).
532	                                                     Specifically, in our BN model, the time of the season correlates with the weather, which
533	                                                     is then associated with the ground condition [54] and injury occurrence[56,57]. As a key
534	                                                     feature of a complex systems approach, the BN can explicitly model the factor interactions/
535	                                                     relationships and query in multiple ways, such as comparing the outcomes of custom RTS
536	                                                     scenarios in the section titled Illustrative application of the BN), understanding the most
537	                                                     influential factors (in the section titled Sensitivity analysis, feature selection and strength

539	                                                     selection and strength of influence).

541	                                                     above factors, so we use an example from the English Premier League (EPL) to illus-
542	                                                     trate the possible correlations. In the EPL, the ground condition tends to be drier in the
543	                                                     preseason. Warm, dry and hard surfaces may be associated with higher injury occur-
544	                                                     rence[56,57], possibly due to a higher level of shoe-surface traction influence [58] and

629	                                           Practical application and future developments
630	                                           The software we used for constructing the BN, GeNIe 2.0, could be used as a decision sup-
631	                                           port tool by sports practitioners, including but not limited to coaches, team managers, sports
632	                                           science and medical staff. Once the BN has been constructed, for example, with the use of
633	                                           GeNIe 2.0, the end users do not need any machine-learning knowledge or advanced computer
634	                                           skills to use the BN. Instead, the only input from the sports practitioners is to collect and
635	                                           input the players’ characteristics into the BN. The new data from every week or season can be
636	                                           input into the system’s database by data scientists (either in-house or third party) to ensure
637	                                           the model is up-to-date. As technology continues to advance, the process of constructing and
638	                                           utilising BN is expected to become easier and more efficient. This increased ease of use may
639	                                           encourage medical staff to invest their efforts in learning and adopting BNs to support their
640	                                           decision-making processes.
641	                                               When planning for RTS for an athlete, the BN can provide a personalised risk analysis
642	                                           from broad epidemiological data, as exemplified in section “Illustrative application of the BN”.
643	                                           While the results of the BN for estimating time to RTS align with existing clinical systems and
644	                                           therefore some practitioners may question the need for a computational decision support tool,
645	                                           it is important to see the potential benefits of integrating BN into sports medical practice in
646	                                           future. Conventional clinical guidelines often apply universally to all individuals regardless of
647	                                           age, sex, sport, or level of play. Consequently, they are not intended to offer an individualised
648	                                           approach to RTS estimation. Given that athletes’ diverse needs and circumstances, coupled
649	                                           with the growing emphasis on personalised and precision medicine, a more tailored approach
650	                                           to estimating RTS becomes essential. In this regard, the incorporation of BN can serve as a
651	                                           valuable addition to sports medical practice to improve decision making.
652	                                               In our example, we explained the use of BN with a RTS scenario and estimated the time to
653	                                           RTS based on a player’s basic characteristics. However, it is important to note that this study
654	                                           is a pilot for future studies, and the potential applications of BN extend beyond this specific
655	                                           use case. They can be leveraged for various purposes, such as forecasting expected perfor-
656	                                           mance or injury risk in a game by considering factors like personal characteristics, opponent
657	                                           playing style, and recent training and game performance. While in this study, the BN yielded
658	                                           similar results to existing clinical systems, its true benefits lie in its ease of use, efficiency, and
659	                                           the capacity to incorporate a wider range of data into the decision-making process. The BN’s
660	                                           ability to identify the strength of influence allows medical staff to address the variables that
661	                                           significantly impact outcomes, a task that cannot be adequately addressed by conventional
662	                                           clinical guidelines alone. By leveraging BN, medical staff may enhance their decision-making
663	                                           processes and provide more tailored and effective care to athletes.

                                           playing style, and recent training and game performance. While in this study, the BN yielded
                                           similar results to existing clinical systems, its true benefits lie in its ease of use, efficiency, and
                                           the capacity to incorporate a wider range of data into the decision-making process. The BN’s
                                           ability to identify the strength of influence allows medical staff to address the variables that
                                           significantly impact outcomes, a task that cannot be adequately addressed by conventional
                                           clinical guidelines alone. By leveraging BN, medical staff may enhance their decision-making
                                           processes and provide more tailored and effective care to athletes.

                                               Computational models are more likely to be implemented in applied sports settings if their
                                           accuracy, interpretability and functionality fit with the operation framework of a sports organ-
                                           isation[61]. In this case, BN provides an intuitive visualisation of the complex relationship of
                                           injuries, which medical staff may understand even with little or no experience in computer
                                           analytics. This may increase the model’s transparency and may improve the medical staff ’s
                                           trust in the model[62]. In terms of practical applicability, medical staff can use the model to
                                           create scenarios that facilitate the evaluation of different management options or the devel-
                                           opment of rehabilitation protocols for players with various positions or injuries occurring
                                           at different times during the season. These scenarios enable the assessment of the combined
                                           effects of risk factors[26]. This may enable them to proactively manage injury risk, and in case
                                           of injury, make more accurate predictions regarding the days to RTS for individual athletes
                                           based on epidemiological evidence. The BN can be modified to suit the specific context as
                                           determined by the user and updated with new information when available. In summary, BNs
                                           seem promising for modelling the relationships of variables in a complex system and may be
                                           further explored to support clinical decision making.
                                               The epidemiological data we used in this study is static; thus, we use a BN to represent the
                                           system as a time-aggregated model. However, most systems, including athletes, have been well
                                           recognised to change over time[4,63]. To capture the change over time and the feedback loops,
                                           a BN can be further extended into a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN)[64]. The DBN is an
                                           extension of the BNs and replicates the BN model at discrete points in time (time slices) and
                                           captures temporal relationships between the variables. DBNs can represent complex ques-
                                           tions, such as how changes in rehabilitation training load affect the time to RTS in athletes
                                           with different demographic and anthropometric characteristics. Modifiable variables, such
                                           as rehabilitation training exposure, can be collected continuously over time as time-series
                                           data[65]. DBNs have been applied in injury prediction[66], medical diagnosis or prognosis
                                           [67–69] and are also a promising avenue for further investigation in subsequent injury risk
                                           modelling. Specifically, DBNs may provide medical practitioners with a tool to predict the
                                           probability of a subsequent injury to occur given time-series data, such as injury history,

702	
703	                                           Limitations
704	                                           The proposed BN model has limitations that should be considered when interpreting its results.
705	                                           Firstly, it is important to recognise that the model was constructed using data solely from the
706	                                           Bundesliga, and therefore, the generalisability of the results to other leagues or levels of play is
707	                                           limited. Second, the quality of the input variables directly impacts the model’s predictive accu-
708	                                           racy. In the case of our BN, it was constructed using basic epidemiological data sourced from
709	                                           public databases. While this approach maximises the availability of injury events for the model,
710	                                           it lacks pertinent information related to prognosis, such as diagnosis (e.g., structural damage or
711	                                           functional disorder) and the precise location of the injury (e.g., involvement of central tendon
712	                                           in hamstring injury) [71]. An accurate diagnosis of an injury plays a vital role in determining
713	                                           prognosis[10,72]. For instance, the recovery time to RTS can vary significantly between a minor
714	                                           partial tear in the hamstring muscle (requiring 17 days to RTS) and a moderate partial tear
715	                                           (requiring a longer time of 36 days to RTS). Therefore, the lack of detailed diagnostic informa-
716	                                           tion can impact the model’s graphical structure and prediction accuracy.
717	                                               Further studies may consider including more information into the model, such as quality
718	                                           and duration of rehabilitation training, RTS performance, reinjury incidence, the importance
719	                                           of upcoming competition, the remaining contract length, the club’s geographical regions
720	                                           and the players’ transfer value. Potentially, depending on the purpose of the model, we can

731	                                              Comparing the machine-learned BN with the existing scientific understanding of injury
732	                                           and recovery would also be a valuable future avenue of research. This comparison can provide
733	                                           insights into the performance and predictive capabilities of a complex model that incorporates
734	                                           a wide range of variables in contrast to a simpler model, such as an epidemiological one. By
735	                                           doing so, researchers can evaluate the added value of BN as a decision-support tool.
736	
737	                                           Conclusion
738	                                           This discrete BN provides a decision support tool to help medical staff, coaches and players
739	                                           manage injury. The BN has a high sensitivity, ranging from 0.73 to 1.00 in predicting severity
740	                                           and provides a graphical representation of the investigated interdependencies. Medical staff
741	                                           can use BN to understand the strength of influence of different variables on the outcome and
742	                                           analyse the outcome based on custom RTS scenarios. This information may help medical staff
743	                                           evaluate different injury scenarios and better respond to individual player’s rehabilitation and
744	                                           team planning. BNs seem promising for modelling the relationships of variables from multiple
745	                                           sources and can be further explored to support clinical decision making.

                                           Limitations
                                           The proposed BN model has limitations that should be considered when interpreting its results.
                                           Firstly, it is important to recognise that the model was constructed using data solely from the
                                           Bundesliga, and therefore, the generalisability of the results to other leagues or levels of play is
                                           limited. Second, the quality of the input variables directly impacts the model’s predictive accu-
                                           racy. In the case of our BN, it was constructed using basic epidemiological data sourced from
                                           public databases. While this approach maximises the availability of injury events for the model,
                                           it lacks pertinent information related to prognosis, such as diagnosis (e.g., structural damage or
                                           functional disorder) and the precise location of the injury (e.g., involvement of central tendon
                                           in hamstring injury) [71]. An accurate diagnosis of an injury plays a vital role in determining
                                           prognosis[10,72]. For instance, the recovery time to RTS can vary significantly between a minor
                                           partial tear in the hamstring muscle (requiring 17 days to RTS) and a moderate partial tear
                                           (requiring a longer time of 36 days to RTS). Therefore, the lack of detailed diagnostic informa-
                                           tion can impact the model’s graphical structure and prediction accuracy.
                                               Further studies may consider including more information into the model, such as quality
                                           and duration of rehabilitation training, RTS performance, reinjury incidence, the importance
                                           of upcoming competition, the remaining contract length, the club’s geographical regions
                                           and the players’ transfer value. Potentially, depending on the purpose of the model, we can



PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0314184 March 20, 2025                                                                      14 / 19

                                           integrate epidemiological data from other larger datasets into the model to enlarge the data-
                                           base to reduce the chance of overfitting and improve result transportability.
                                              Comparing the machine-learned BN with the existing scientific understanding of injury
                                           and recovery would also be a valuable future avenue of research. This comparison can provide
                                           insights into the performance and predictive capabilities of a complex model that incorporates
                                           a wide range of variables in contrast to a simpler model, such as an epidemiological one. By
                                           doing so, researchers can evaluate the added value of BN as a decision-support tool.

                                           Conclusion
                                           This discrete BN provides a decision support tool to help medical staff, coaches and players
                                           manage injury. The BN has a high sensitivity, ranging from 0.73 to 1.00 in predicting severity
                                           and provides a graphical representation of the investigated interdependencies. Medical staff
                                           can use BN to understand the strength of influence of different variables on the outcome and
                                           analyse the outcome based on custom RTS scenarios. This information may help medical staff
                                           evaluate different injury scenarios and better respond to individual player’s rehabilitation and
                                           team planning. BNs seem promising for modelling the relationships of variables from multiple
                                           sources and can be further explored to support clinical decision making.

34	                                                               This study aimed to investigate the recovery of neuromuscular performance using mechanical parameters collected during
35	                                                               jump (vertical and horizontal) and strength-power exercises in youth soccer players after official soccer matches. Twenty-one
36	                                                               outfield highly trained youth male soccer athletes (age: 18.23 ± 0.73 years; weight: 72.12 ± 6.99 kg; height: 1.78 ± 0.08 m)
37	                                                               from two teams competing in the 1st division of U-19 Portuguese National Championship participated in this study. Players
38	                                                               completed a battery of physical tests at -2h, +30 min, +24h, and +48h in relation to the match. Countermovement jump height,
39	                                                               horizontal jump distance, and bar velocity during the half-squat, bench press, and hip-thrust exercises, at fixed loads, were
40	                                                               recorded. Countermovement jump was impaired until 24h post-match (-1.7% from pre to 24h post, p=0.050; ES=-0.82). Half-

43	                                                               ES=-0.80). No impairments were found in the horizontal jump and bench press at any moment. Our findings show prolonged
44	                                                               decrements in strength of the posterior chain following a soccer match, measured in the hip-thrust exercise, while the other
45	                                                               exercises displayed faster recovery dynamics.

                                                               Abstract:
                                                               This study aimed to investigate the recovery of neuromuscular performance using mechanical parameters collected during
                                                               jump (vertical and horizontal) and strength-power exercises in youth soccer players after official soccer matches. Twenty-one
                                                               outfield highly trained youth male soccer athletes (age: 18.23 ± 0.73 years; weight: 72.12 ± 6.99 kg; height: 1.78 ± 0.08 m)
                                                               from two teams competing in the 1st division of U-19 Portuguese National Championship participated in this study. Players
                                                               completed a battery of physical tests at -2h, +30 min, +24h, and +48h in relation to the match. Countermovement jump height,
                                                               horizontal jump distance, and bar velocity during the half-squat, bench press, and hip-thrust exercises, at fixed loads, were
                                                               recorded. Countermovement jump was impaired until 24h post-match (-1.7% from pre to 24h post, p=0.050; ES=-0.82). Half-
                                                               squat bar velocity was reduced immediately following the match (-6.8 % from pre- p=0.004; ES=-0.64) but recovered at +24h
                                                               (+2.9%, p=1.00; ES=0.02). Hip-thrust bar velocity was reduced for up to 48h post-match (-7.4% from pre to 48h post, p<0.001;
                                                               ES=-0.80). No impairments were found in the horizontal jump and bench press at any moment. Our findings show prolonged
                                                               decrements in strength of the posterior chain following a soccer match, measured in the hip-thrust exercise, while the other
                                                               exercises displayed faster recovery dynamics.

                                                               268   0.80). Contrary to what was hypothesized [16], decreases in half-squat bar velocity were




                                                                                                                                                                Accepted Manuscript
                                                               269   only significant following the match (-6.8% from pre- to post-match, ; p = 0.004; ES = -

                                                               270   0.64), returning to baseline after 24h (+2.9%, p=1.00; ES=0.02). Additionally, no

                                                               271   significant differences were observed in the HJ d and bench press bar velocity from pre-

                                                               272   to post-match time points, except for an improved HJd at 48h post-match. Due to the

                                                               273   high loading of the posterior chain during soccer matches, it was hypothesized that

                                                               274   movements primarily recruiting the gluteus maximus and hamstrings would take longer

                                                               275   time to recover. This was partially confirmed by our data showing that reductions in the

                                                               276   hip-thrust bar velocity persisted for 48h after the match.


                                                               277   In line with previous studies [2,5,18], soccer matches resulted in impaired

                                                               278   neuromuscular performance that persisted for 24-48h post-match. CMJh in the current

                                                               279   study declined post-match (6.79%) and at 24h but recovered just after 48h. These results

                                                               280   diverge from existing evidence at the post-48h time point. For instance, de Hoyo et al.

                                                               281   [5] reported a peak decrease in CMJh after 24h, but performance remained impaired at

                                                               282   48h post-match. Similarly, Nedelec et al. [18] showed an ~7.5% decrease in jump
                                                                283   height 48h after a match in senior professional soccer players. Finally, Magalhães et al.

                                                               284   [33] reported an ~12% CMJh decrease at 48h. Several studies did not observe any

                                                               285   meaningful changes in CMJh following competition or intermittent exercise [14,34].

                                                               286   Thus, it could be argued that CMJh alone may not be sensitive enough to measure acute

                                                               287   or residual neuromuscular fatigue [14,34], at least in conditions of relatively low

                                                               288   fatigue, as was probably the case at +48h post-match. Furthermore, there is a possibility

                                                               289   that athletes can maintain jump height even under the presence of fatigue by increasing




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               290   the length of the CMJ eccentric phase or the CMJ total contraction time [5]. Thus, there

                                                               291   seems to exist substantial variability in the CMJ h decreases following real or simulated




                                                                                                                                                                               Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               292   soccer matches or other high-intensity and intermittent sports. Additionally, it is

                                                               293   important to consider that Nedelec et al. [18] analyzed professional senior soccer




                                                                                                                                                                  Accepted Manuscript
                                                               294   players and Magalhães et al. [33] investigated senior professional and semi-professional

                                                               295   soccer players. Nonetheless, our results agree with those reported by Brownstein et al.

                                                               296   [1] showing that CMJh decreased immediately post- and 24h after a match, but returned

                                                               297   to baseline values at 48h, aligning with measures of central and peripheral fatigue.


                                                               298   Regarding the half-squat, a 5.05% decrease in MPV was noted, but performance was

                                                               299   recovered after just 24h. Callaghan et al. [16] have used a similar approach in rugby

                                                               300   players. The authors found significant decrements in the back squat mean velocity at 30

                                                               301   min, 24h, and 48h post-match. However, there are methodological differences between

                                                               302   the studies. The authors of that study used a different and lighter load, corresponding to

                                                               303   a mean velocity of 1m.s-1 (V1load). In our study, the “baseline” (pre-match) MPV was

                                                               304   slower (0.69 ± 0.1 m.s-1), which means that the load lifted was relatively heavier,

                                                               305   corresponding to ~70% of the e1RM. Additionally, the aforementioned authors

                                                               306   hypothesized that the greater range of motion and stretch on the impaired musculature

                                                               307   resulting from the squat (femurs approximately parallel to the floor during the eccentric
                                                                308   portion of the exercise) may have contributed to the detection of neuromuscular fatigue.

                                                               309   Furthermore, it is worth mentioning that, compared to soccer, rugby is likely more

                                                               310   physically demanding in terms of physical contact. In addition, heavy rugby players

                                                               311   apply very high eccentric forces during decelerations due to their sprint momentum

                                                               312   [35]. Short high-intensity actions such as accelerations/decelerations, and sprinting are

                                                               313   commonly observed in soccer matches and have been associated with muscle damage,

                                                               314   thus affecting subsequent recovery kinetics [18,36]. Decreases in maximum voluntary




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               315   contraction torque associated with muscle damage have been extensively studied [6,11]

                                                               316   and seem to be a consequence of impairments in contractile function and/or the capacity




                                                                                                                                                                               Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               317   of the central nervous system to effectively activate the muscle [1]. It seems that muscle

                                                               318   damage and fatigue are attenuated in less than 24h for the half-squat exercise in young




                                                                                                                                                                  Accepted Manuscript
                                                               319   soccer players, allowing them to use this exercise early in the competitive schedule

                                                               320   (e.g., MD+1).


                                                               321   In contrast with the time course of the half-squat, performance in the hip-thrust exercise

                                                               322   was impaired from post-match up to 48h. Greater impairments in the hamstring muscles

                                                               323   compared to the quadriceps have been shown to prevail up to 72h post-match [2].

                                                               324   Accordingly, decrements in neuromuscular performance and increases in muscle

                                                               325   soreness of the hamstrings have been previously reported following soccer-simulated

                                                               326   intermittent running exercises and other team sports’ matches with high eccentric

                                                               327   components [37,38]. An increase in soccer training-related hamstring injury rates has

                                                               328   been reported, in comparison to competition-related injuries [39], and this might be

                                                               329   related to the increased match demands and/or players experiencing high training loads

                                                               330   during recovery periods [2]. Furthermore, given that gluteus maximum is highly taxed

                                                               331   during soccer specific actions (e.g., sprint) [40], prolonged post-match fatigue/damage

                                                               332   in this muscle likely help explain the recovery kinetics of hip-thrust, an exercise that
                                                                333   highly activates the gluteus [41]. Since muscle damage and fatigue in the hip-thrust

                                                               334   persists for at least 48h following the match, exercises/movements that place more

                                                               335   mechanical stress on the gluteus and hamstring muscles should be avoided at MD+1 and

                                                               336   MD+2.


                                                               337   On the other hand, bar velocity in the bench press exercise remained constant

                                                               338   throughout the post-match period. Thus, upper body resistance training (at least pushing




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               339   exercises such as the bench press) on the days following a match might be feasible.

                                                               340   Scheduling upper body resistance training might help preserving upper body strength

                                                               341   [10]. Since upper-body resistance training seems to fit in the first sessions post-match,




                                                                                                                                                                              Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               342   exercises such as bench press can be easily implemented in the competitive microcycle,




                                                                                                                                                                 Accepted Manuscript
                                                               343   especially due to the role of upper body in actions such as sprinting and body contacts

                                                               344   [21].


                                                               345   Lastly, HJ performance did not decrease across the observed period and even an

                                                               346   increase in HJ distance was observed at 48h post-match. The hip-thrust and HJ exercises

                                                               347   share some similarities, with both movements being performed using the anteroposterior

                                                               348   force-vector [42]. Thus, it was initially hypothesized that both exercises would follow

                                                               349   similar recovery kinetics after the match. However, it is worth mentioning that force

                                                               350   application differs substantially between them, since the HJ is a very fast horizontally

                                                               351   oriented movement performed without external loading. In contrast, the hip-thrust was

                                                               352   executed at a moderate-to-high loading condition (~70% of e1RM). Furthermore, even

                                                               353   though players were instructed to maintain a similar jumping technique during all

                                                               354   assessments, a change in technique to accommodate the resultant fatigue is a possibility.

                                                               355   Similarly, familiarization to the HJ during testing sessions cannot be ruled out;

                                                               356   however, all players performed HJs regularly in their clubs. According to our results,
                                                                357   unloaded HJs may be performed on the day following the match or even combined with

                                                               358   CMJs 48h post-match (MD+2/-4).


                                                               359


                                                               360   LIMITATIONS


                                                               361   Our study has some limitations. First, because the study was conducted during the

                                                                     competitive season, using the traditional approach to determine the 1RM load was not




This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.
                                                               362

                                                               363   possible. Therefore, a submaximal load was selected to avoid unnecessary risks and

                                                               364   fatigue when lifting heavier loads [22]. A larger sample size with a longer follow-up




                                                                                                                                                                               Downloaded by: University of Cincinnati. Copyrighted material.
                                                               365   period (more athletes and more matches) could allow different sub-analyzes (i.e.,




                                                                                                                                                                  Accepted Manuscript
                                                               366   starters vs. non-starters, stronger vs. weaker athletes) across multiple time-points. The

                                                               367   order of the exercises performed was not randomized, and this could also be considered

                                                               368   a limitation. Lastly, only the external match loads were monitored, without considering

                                                               369   training loads and well-being status throughout the week.


                                                               370


                                                               371   CONCLUSION


                                                               372   In conclusion, the posterior chain strength as measured by the hip-thrust exercise takes

                                                               373   more than 48h to recover after a match. This means that prescribing such exercise

                                                               374   during strength-power training sessions deserves caution on MD+1 and MD+2. Other

                                                               375   loaded exercises, such as the half-squat, is fully recovered after the 24h post-match,

                                                               376   while performance in the bench press is not affected by the match. Hence, these

                                                               377   exercises can be programmed in the first days interspersing two consecutive matches.

                                                               378   Finally, HJ performance is immediately recovered after the match, while CMJh takes

                                                               379   only 48h to return to baseline values. This finding indicates that plyometric exercises in
                                                                380   the post-match days can stress first the horizontal (MD+1) and later the vertical force

                                                               381   vector (MD+2 on) within a competitive youth soccer microcycle.

                                                                                Young Soccer Players
                                                                                                       Using Bar Velocity to Assess Post-match Neuromuscular Fatigue in
                                                                4    Abstract
                                                               5    This study aimed to investigate the recovery of neuromuscular performance using
                                                               6    mechanical parameters collected during jump (vertical and horizontal) and strength-
                                                               7    power exercises in youth soccer players after official soccer matches. This study aimed
                                                               8    to quantify the changes in the concentric mean propulsive velocity of the barbell half-
                                                               9    squat, bench press and hip-thrust, and in the performance of the countermovement jump
                                                               10   and horizontal jump, after a soccer match in youth players. Twenty-one outfield highly
                                                               11   trained youth male soccer athletes (age: 18.23 ± 0.73 years; weight: 72.12 ± 6.99 kg;
                                                               12   height: 1.78 ± 0.08 m) from two teams competing in the 1st division of U-19 Portuguese
                                                               13   National Championship participated in this study. Players completed a battery of
                                                               14   physical tests at -2h, +30 min, +24h, and +48h in relation to the match.
                                                               15   Countermovement jump height, horizontal jump distance, and bar velocity during the
                                                               16   resistance exerciseshalf-squat, bench press, and hip-thrust exercises, at fixed loads, were
                                                               17   recorded. Countermovement jump was impaired until 24h post-match (-1.7% from pre
                                                               18   to 24h post, p=0.050; ES=-0.82). Half-squat bar velocity was reduced immediately
                                                               19   following the match (-6.85. 05% from pre- p=0.004; ES=-0.64) but recovered at +24h
                                                               20   (+2.9%, p=1.00; ES=0.02). Hip-thrust bar velocity was reduced for up to 48h post-
                                                               21   match (-7.4% from pre to 48h post, p<0.001; ES=-0.80). No impairments were found in
                                                               22   the horizontal jump and bench press at any moment. Our findings show prolonged
                                                               23   decrements in strength of the posterior chain following a soccer match, measured in the
                                                               24   hip-thrust exercise, while the other exercises displayed faster recovery dynamics.
                                                               26   Keywords: team sports; recovery; strength training; mean concentric velocity
                                                                27   INTRODUCTION
                                                               28   Soccer players deal with very-high physical demands during matches that are related to
                                                               29   acute and delayed manifestations of fatigue [1,2]. In fact, high-intensity activities are
                                                               30   progressively reduced toward the end of the second half of the match [3,4] and physical
                                                               31   performance is impaired immediately after competitive soccer matches [1,5]. This

  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Use bar-velocity tracking during routine lifts to check readiness at MD+1 and MD+2 without an extra test. Sequence exercises so hip-thrust is not the first loaded lift on the day after a match, because it was still reduced at 48 h.",

Methods: The total study sample was 93 participants (female, n = 47), recruited from two

 INTRODUCTION

        It is well established that inadequate fluid intake adversely affects physical and

psychological performance on the short-term (i.e., acute dehydration), and may increase the risk

of chronic disease long-term (i.e., poor fluid intake behaviors). Thus, efforts to adequately assess

hydration status allow for a direct means of addressing changes in total body water. A plethora of

methods used to determine or capture changes in hydration status are succinctly summarized in


                                                                            D
previous literature (1). While laboratory or field-based methods for hydration assessment in

research settings provide accurate measures of body water regulation and homeostasis, these




                            EP
measures are not feasible in the general population. Cheuvront and Sawka (2) proposed a

framework that includes morning body weight (W), first urine void color (U), and thirst




                              TE
perception (T; WUT framework) as a simple approach for laypersons to determine the adequacy

of their fluid intake. Individual changes in W (>1% body mass, kg), U (>5 A.U. using a 1 – 8-

point urine color chart (3)), and T (conscious desire to consume fluids) provide evidence of

inadequate fluid intake; however, a combination of changes that exceed these thresholds further

strengthens the likelihood of insufficient fluid intake.

and the individual variables included in the model. Once body weight decreases by 1% of overall



A

intake, rather than sensible and insensible fluid loss. Similarly, as TBW decreases, plasma

osmolality increases, triggering internal mechanisms responsible for the presence of thirst (4),

and renal water retention increases in response to increasing arginine vasopressin (AVP)

concentrations – thereby concentrating the urine. This increase in urine concentration can be

osmolality and urine specific gravity (3).

validity of using this framework has not been fully explored. Sekiguchi and colleagues (5)

manipulation protocol where body water is actively lost from the body (i.e., sweating), a design

that allows for the direct assessment of the efficacy of the proposed model. Importantly, this

previous work considered WUT components as binary predictors (i.e., value exceeds a threshold

or not), rather than treating each component as a continuous measure that can linearly or non-

linearly change with the likelihood of dehydration. Lastly, as evidenced in the work of Sekiguchi

et el., Keefe et al., and Wardenaar et al., the WUT framework assumes that each component

contributes equally to determining the likelihood of dehydration. Although this conjecture is



A
reasonable based on the originally proposed model, it is unlikely to be accurate, since the

sensitivity of each WUT component for predicting dehydration differs in reference to body water

regulation, suggesting unequal weighting is likely.

predictive model provides individuals a better understanding as to which of these variables offers

14	Background: The Vestibular/Ocular-Motor Screening (VOMS) is a valuable component of acute (\72 hours) sports-related con-
15	cussion (SRC) assessments and is increasingly used with the Immediate Post-concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing
16	(ImPACT) instrument and the third edition of the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT3). Research has suggested that
17	VOMS acute postinjury scores are useful in identifying acute concussion. However, the utility of preseason baseline measure-
18	ments to improve diagnostic accuracy remains ambiguous. To this end, there is a need to determine how reliable VOMS baseline
19	assessments are across years and whether incorporating individuals’ baseline performance improves diagnostic yield for acute
20	concussions.
21	Purpose: To analyze VOMS, SCAT3, and ImPACT to evaluate the test-retest reliability of consecutive-year preseason baseline
22	assessments to directly compare the diagnostic utility of these tools when incorporating baseline assessments versus using post-
23	injury data alone to identify acute SRC.
24	Study Design: Cohort study (diagnosis); Level of evidence, 2.
25	Methods: Preseason and postinjury VOMS, SCAT3, ImPACT Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS), and ImPACT composite
26	scores were analyzed for 3958 preseason (47.7% female) and 496 acute (48 hours) SRC (37.5% female) collegiate athlete eval-
27	uations in the National Collegiate Athletic Association—Department of Defense Concussion Assessment Research and Education
28	Consortium. Descriptive statistics, Kolmogorov-Smirnov significance, and Cohen d effect size were calculated. Consecutive-year
29	baseline reliability was evaluated for a subset of 447 athlete encounters using Pearson r, Cohen k, Cohen d, and 2-way mixed
30	intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Wilcoxon signed rank tests were used to determine the statistical significance between
31	population performances, and the 90% reliable change index (RCI) was calculated from the test-retest results. Preseason to post-
32	injury change scores were then calculated from each tool’s RCI. Finally, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses
33	were conducted, and DeLong method was used to compare the area under the curve (AUC) of raw postinjury scores versus
34	change scores from preseason baseline assessments. Potential effects of sex, medical history (learning disorders or attention-
35	deficit/hyperactivity disorder), and outlier data were also explored.
36	Results: Effect sizes were large, and overall predictive utilities were clinically useful for postinjury VOMS Total (d = 2.44; AUC =
37	0.85), the SCAT3 Symptom Evaluation total severity score (d = 1.74; AUC = 0.82), and the ImPACT PCSS total severity score (d =
38	1.67; AUC = 0.80). Comparatively, effect sizes were small and predictive utilities were poor for Standardized Assessment of Con-
39	cussion (SAC), modified Balance Error Scoring System (mBESS), and all ImPACT composites (d = 0.11-0.46; AUC = 0.48-0.59).
40	Preseason baseline test-retest reliability was poor to moderate (r = 0.23-0.52; k = 0.32-0.36; ICC = 0.36-0.68) for all assessments

Utility of VOMS, SCAT3, and ImPACT
Baseline Evaluations for Acute Concussion
Identification in Collegiate Athletes
Findings From the NCAA-DoD Concussion Assessment,
Research and Education (CARE) Consortium
Lyndsey M. Ferris,* PhD, OD, Anthony P. Kontos,y PhD, Shawn R. Eagle,y PhD, ATC ,
R.J. Elbin,z PhD, Michael W. Collins,y PhD, Anne Mucha,§ DPT, MS, NCS,
Thomas W. McAllister,|| MD, AB, Steven P. Broglio,{ PhD, ATC, Michael McCrea,# PHD, ABPP,
Paul F. Pasquina,** MD, and Nicholas L. Port,*yy PhD
Investigation performed at Humboldt State University, Indiana University, University of Delaware,
University of North Carolina, West Chester University, Wake Forest University, University of
Wisconsin-Madison, Winston-Salem State University

Background: The Vestibular/Ocular-Motor Screening (VOMS) is a valuable component of acute (\72 hours) sports-related con-
cussion (SRC) assessments and is increasingly used with the Immediate Post-concussion Assessment and Cognitive Testing
(ImPACT) instrument and the third edition of the Sport Concussion Assessment Tool (SCAT3). Research has suggested that
VOMS acute postinjury scores are useful in identifying acute concussion. However, the utility of preseason baseline measure-
ments to improve diagnostic accuracy remains ambiguous. To this end, there is a need to determine how reliable VOMS baseline
assessments are across years and whether incorporating individuals’ baseline performance improves diagnostic yield for acute
concussions.
Purpose: To analyze VOMS, SCAT3, and ImPACT to evaluate the test-retest reliability of consecutive-year preseason baseline
assessments to directly compare the diagnostic utility of these tools when incorporating baseline assessments versus using post-
injury data alone to identify acute SRC.
Study Design: Cohort study (diagnosis); Level of evidence, 2.
Methods: Preseason and postinjury VOMS, SCAT3, ImPACT Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS), and ImPACT composite
scores were analyzed for 3958 preseason (47.7% female) and 496 acute (48 hours) SRC (37.5% female) collegiate athlete eval-
uations in the National Collegiate Athletic Association—Department of Defense Concussion Assessment Research and Education
Consortium. Descriptive statistics, Kolmogorov-Smirnov significance, and Cohen d effect size were calculated. Consecutive-year
baseline reliability was evaluated for a subset of 447 athlete encounters using Pearson r, Cohen k, Cohen d, and 2-way mixed
intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Wilcoxon signed rank tests were used to determine the statistical significance between
population performances, and the 90% reliable change index (RCI) was calculated from the test-retest results. Preseason to post-
injury change scores were then calculated from each tool’s RCI. Finally, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses
were conducted, and DeLong method was used to compare the area under the curve (AUC) of raw postinjury scores versus
change scores from preseason baseline assessments. Potential effects of sex, medical history (learning disorders or attention-
deficit/hyperactivity disorder), and outlier data were also explored.
Results: Effect sizes were large, and overall predictive utilities were clinically useful for postinjury VOMS Total (d = 2.44; AUC =
0.85), the SCAT3 Symptom Evaluation total severity score (d = 1.74; AUC = 0.82), and the ImPACT PCSS total severity score (d =
1.67; AUC = 0.80). Comparatively, effect sizes were small and predictive utilities were poor for Standardized Assessment of Con-
cussion (SAC), modified Balance Error Scoring System (mBESS), and all ImPACT composites (d = 0.11-0.46; AUC = 0.48-0.59).
Preseason baseline test-retest reliability was poor to moderate (r = 0.23-0.52; k = 0.32-0.36; ICC = 0.36-0.68) for all assessments

except ImPACT Visual Motion Sensitivity (r = 0.73; ICC = 0.85). Incorporating baseline scores for VOMS Total, SCAT3 (Symptom
Evaluation, SAC, mBESS), ImPACT PCSS, or ImPACT composites did not significantly improve AUCs.
Conclusion: VOMS Total and symptom severity (SCAT3, PCSS) total scores had large effect sizes and clinically useful AUCs for
identifying acute concussion. However, all tools demonstrated high within-patient test-retest variability, resulting in poor reliability.
The findings in this sample of collegiate athletes suggest that incorporating baseline assessments does not significantly increase
diagnostic yield for acute concussion.
Keywords: sport-related concussion; VOMS; SCAT; ImPACT; Reliable Change Index

 "sourceFile": "Utility of VOMS, SCAT3, and ImPACT baseline evaluations for acute concussion identification in collegaite athletes - Findings from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium.pdf",

 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Brain Health & Psychology", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Collegiate", "Male Athletes", "Female Athletes", "Healthy Athletes", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Cohort analysis from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium of 3958 preseason and 496 acute (48 hour) concussion evaluations in collegiate athletes and cadets, with 447 consecutive-year baseline pairs for test-retest reliability. The VOMS Total score (AUC 0.85), SCAT3 Symptom Evaluation (AUC 0.82) and ImPACT PCSS (AUC 0.80) discriminated concussion well from raw post-injury scores, but test-retest reliability was poor to moderate and adding preseason change scores did not improve AUC (VOMS Total decreased).",
 "screeningLimitations": "The sample is mostly NCAA Division I athletes, and the analyses depended on RCI and Pearson-based methods applied to largely non-normal data, which the authors acknowledge. Results are limited to these tools and to the CARE sites, so they cannot be generalised to other tools, levels or age groups.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the paper as showing that preseason baseline testing is useless for concussion care, when it shows that baseline change scores did not add accuracy to these specific tools in this sample, and that raw post-injury scores still discriminate well.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2022,
  "citation": "Ferris LM, Kontos AP, Eagle SR, et al. Utility of VOMS, SCAT3, and ImPACT baseline evaluations for acute concussion identification in collegiate athletes: findings from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium. Am J Sports Med. 2022:1-14.",
  "doi": "10.1177/03635465211072261",
  "abstract": "The authors compared raw post-injury scores with preseason change scores for the VOMS, SCAT3 and ImPACT in collegiate athletes from the NCAA-DoD CARE Consortium. Raw VOMS, SCAT3 symptom and ImPACT symptom scores identified concussion well, test-retest reliability was poor to moderate, and incorporating baseline performance did not significantly improve accuracy.",
  "tldr": "Post-injury symptom scores from the VOMS, SCAT3 and ImPACT identify concussion well on their own. Adding preseason baseline change scores did not improve accuracy, so the value of routine baseline testing for these tools is limited.",
  "methods": "The study used CARE Consortium data from NCAA and military academy athletes. It analysed 3958 preseason and 496 acute evaluations, calculated consecutive-year test-retest reliability in 447 pairs, derived reliable change indices, and compared raw post-injury scores with preseason change scores using ROC curves, the Youden method and DeLong tests.",
  "findings": "Post-injury VOMS Total (d = 2.44; AUC 0.85), SCAT3 Symptom Evaluation (d = 1.74; AUC 0.82) and ImPACT PCSS (d = 1.67; AUC 0.80) had large effect sizes and useful discrimination. SAC, mBESS and ImPACT composites had small effects and poor AUCs. Test-retest reliability was poor to moderate for most measures (for VOMS Total r = 0.23, ICC 0.36), and change scores did not improve AUCs, with VOMS Total significantly reduced.",
  "limitations": "Most participants came from NCAA Division I programmes, and the population may not represent other athletes or age groups. Symptom reports are subjective and motivation at baseline may vary, and the authors used parametric reliability methods on mostly non-normal data. The abstract gives an AUC range of 0.48 to 0.59 for the weaker measures, while the results give 0.48 to 0.60.",
  "practicalImplications": "Interpret post-injury VOMS, SCAT3 symptom and ImPACT PCSS scores against normative values rather than an individual preseason change score for these tools. Weigh the cost of routine preseason baseline concussion testing against the small gain in accuracy it gave in this sample.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Not applicable to training or performance planning. The study concerns concussion identification, and it does not measure training, fitness or performance outcomes.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study does not address return-to-play decisions or recovery time. It supports using post-injury symptom and vestibular-ocular scores as part of the acute concussion evaluation, but it does not establish criteria for when an athlete can return."
 }
}

{
 "id": "Q33",
 "sourceFile": "Utility of Body Weight, Urine Color, and Thirst Perception (WUT) in Determining Hydration in Young Adults.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Text title 'Utility of Body Weight, Urine Color, and Thirst Perception (WUT) in Determining Hydration in Young Adults' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Methodological / Validation Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Nutrition & Hydration",
 "domains": ["Nutrition & Hydration", "Monitoring & Technology"],
 "audiences": ["Nutrition", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Two free-living cohorts (Study 1, 58 participants for 3 days; Study 2, 35 participants for 7 days) of healthy adults aged 18 to 35 (93 total, 47 female) provided reference change values for body mass, urine color and thirst, then Study 2 underwent 2 hours of passive heating followed by random assignment to control, sweat-loss or fluid-restriction conditions. Body mass change, urine color and thirst each separated the groups for predicted dehydration probability, and ridge regression gave body mass 58% and thirst 26% of relative importance in the weighted WUT model.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Participants were healthy, non-athlete young adults who exercised no more than 10 hours a week, and the authors say results may not transfer to athletes, older adults or people with illness. The model was fitted and tested on the same data without a holdout set, and the authors caution that the importance weights may be overfitted.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could take the 58% and 26% weightings or the 90% dehydration probabilities as validated athlete hydration thresholds, when they come from healthy non-athlete adults in a 2-hour heat and fluid-restriction protocol, with no athlete data.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Adams WM, Anderson T, Zaplatosch ME, et al. Utility of Body Weight, Urine Color, and Thirst Perception (WUT) in Determining Hydration in Young Adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024 (published ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000003514",
  "abstract": "The authors tested the body weight, urine color and thirst (WUT) hydration framework in 93 young adults. Using reference change values and a 2-hour passive heating and fluid manipulation protocol, they found that body mass change and thirst were the most important predictors of dehydration, and they proposed a weighted version of the WUT model.",
  "tldr": "In healthy young adults, a change in morning body mass or thirst was the strongest signal of dehydration, with urine color adding less. A weighted WUT model may help people judge whether they need more fluid, but it has not been tested in athletes.",
  "methods": "Phase 1 collected 24-hour and first-morning urine, body mass and thirst ratings over 3 days (Study 1, n = 58) or 7 days (Study 2, n = 35) of free-living life. Reference change values were computed for each WUT component. In Study 2, participants then completed a 2-hour seated passive heat exposure (40 C, 50% relative humidity) and were randomised to control, sweat-loss or fluid-restriction conditions, with dehydration probability compared by ANOVA and ridge regression used to weight the components.",
  "findings": "After the manipulation, body mass change (-0.0%, -1.19%, -1.49% in control, sweat-loss and restriction) and thirst separated the groups for predicted dehydration probability (p = 0.001 and p < 0.001). Urine color separated restriction from control (p = 0.044). Ridge regression explained 83% of variance, with body mass 58%, thirst 26% and the body mass by urine color and body mass by thirst interactions 5% each. The authors report that a 1% body mass change and a 1-unit thirst change each corresponded to a high probability of dehydration.",
  "limitations": "Participants were healthy young adults who exercised 10 hours a week or less, so the reference values and weights may not apply to athletes, older adults or patients. Adherence to the fluid restriction was not verified and no participant was excluded, the regression used all data without a validation split, and the authors call for confirmation of the coefficients in other populations.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use morning body mass change and first-morning thirst as the main day-to-day checks for fluid adequacy, with urine color as a supporting measure. Treat a body mass change above about 1% of normal body mass as a cue to drink more, consistent with the authors' recommendation.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The model could give athletes and staff a simple daily hydration check before training or competition. It was tested in healthy non-athletes who did not train heavily, so applying it to athletes needs its own validation before it guides fluid plans.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study does not include injured or recovering athletes and does not address return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to judge fluid status during rehabilitation or return to play."
 }
}

  "tldr": "The heat tolerance test is used to help decide when people can return after exertional heat stroke, but it has not been shown to predict recovery or recurrence. Use it as one input alongside clinical markers and gradual return, not as a stand-alone clearance test.",

  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Heat acclimatisation and fitness affect heat tolerance, so return-to-training plans after heat illness should build load gradually and in the heat.  "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Two free-living cohorts (Study 1, 58 participants for 3 days; Study 2, 35 participants for 7 days) of healthy adults aged 18 to 35 (93 total, 47 female) provided reference change values for body mass, urine color and thirst, then Study 2 underwent 2 hours of passive heating followed by random assignment to control, sweat-loss or fluid-restriction conditions.  "screeningLimitations": "Participants were healthy, non-athlete young adults who exercised no more than 10 hours a week, and the authors say results may not transfer to athletes, older adults or people with illness.  "synthesisCaution": "Staff could take the 58% and 26% weightings or the 90% dehydration probabilities as validated athlete hydration thresholds, when they come from healthy non-athlete adults in a 2-hour heat and fluid-restriction protocol, with no athlete data.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Adams WM, Anderson T, Zaplatosch ME, et al. Utility of Body Weight, Urine Color, and Thirst Perception (WUT) in Determining Hydration in Young Adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024 (published ahead of print).",
  "doi": "10.1249/MSS.0000000000003514",
  "abstract": "The authors tested the body weight, urine color and thirst (WUT) hydration framework in 93 young adults. Using reference change values and a 2-hour passive heating and fluid manipulation protocol, they found that body mass change and thirst were the most important predictors of dehydration, and they proposed a weighted version of the WUT model.",
  "tldr": "In healthy young adults, a change in morning body mass or thirst was the strongest signal of dehydration, with urine color adding less. A weighted WUT model may help people judge whether they need more fluid, but it has not been tested in athletes.",
  "methods": "Phase 1 collected 24-hour and first-morning urine, body mass and thirst ratings over 3 days (Study 1, n = 58) or 7 days (Study 2, n = 35) of free-living life. Reference change values were computed for each WUT component. In Study 2, participants then completed a 2-hour seated passive heat exposure (40 C, 50% relative humidity) and were randomised to control, sweat-loss or fluid-restriction conditions, with dehydration probability compared by ANOVA and ridge regression used to weight the components.",
  "findings": "After the manipulation, body mass change (-0.0%, -1.19%, -1.49% in control, sweat-loss and restriction) and thirst separated the groups for predicted dehydration probability (p = 0.001 and p < 0.001). Urine color separated restriction from control (p = 0.044). Ridge regression explained 83% of variance, with body mass 58%, thirst 26% and the body mass by urine color and body mass by thirst interactions 5% each. The authors report that a body mass change of about 1% was more likely or very likely to indicate dehydration, and a 1-unit thirst change gave a 90% probability.",
  "limitations": "Participants were healthy young adults who exercised 10 hours a week or less, so the reference values and weights may not apply to athletes, older adults or patients. Adherence to the fluid restriction was not verified and no participant was excluded, the regression used all data without a validation split, and the authors call for confirmation of the coefficients in other populations.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use morning body mass change and first-morning thirst as the main day-to-day checks for fluid adequacy, with urine color as a supporting measure. Treat a body mass change above about 1% of normal body mass as a cue to drink more, consistent with the authors' recommendation.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: The model could give athletes and staff a simple daily hydration check before training or competition. It was tested in healthy non-athletes who did not train heavily, so applying it to athletes needs its own validation before it guides fluid plans.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study does not include injured or recovering athletes and does not address return-to-play decisions. It cannot be used to judge fluid status during rehabilitation or return to play."
 }
}
